doc.title: Sam Most interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 15, 1999

title: Standards repertoire for casuals and rock and roll
summary: The standards learned from radio for bar mitzvahs and weddings; rock and roll had not yet reached his gigs.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: When you were doing the bar mitzvahs and the gigs to pay the rent, you were kind of expected to know a certain—

Oh yeah. Well as I say you kind of grew up with all the standards and that was part of the thing other than if you had to play some ethnic Jewish stuff for the bar mitzvahs. Otherwise you know you just would hear the tunes on the radio. “I Hear a Rhapsody” or whatever that they might play at some of these gigs. Some of the tunes of the Latin stuff, “What a Difference a Day Made,” and it became part of your repertoire, all the standards that you heard on the radio that were current at the time. That was before, what do you call it, “I Get No Satisfaction.”
You hinted at my next question, you know if any of the early rock & roll, if you began to get requests for that kind of thing on those gigs, and how did you deal with that?

Actually I think I left before then or else it wasn’t, maybe it was coming. I knew that was becoming more popular. I think other people were doing it or else I didn’t get too much, especially on my instrument — maybe you had to do it more on guitar or something else.
